title: PHP2Shell Vulnerabilities Explained in My Own Words
excerpt: Hackers getting into websites without a password? Here's what actually went wrong inside PHP, explained simply with interactive visuals.
content:
[callout:key](**TL;DR**: PHP2Shell isn't a "skip the password" trick. It's two memory bugs inside PHP itself that, under the right conditions, can let an attacker run their own code on a web server.)

You've probably come across PHP2Shell by now: websites going offline, organisations issuing security warnings, administrators taking their systems down to protect them.

And all we keep hearing on Instagram Reels is *"hackers can access a website without even needing a password."*

Okay, but **how**? What's actually happening behind the scenes? Let's go a little deeper 👇

---

## 🐘 First, what is PHP?

PHP is a programming language widely used to build websites and web applications.

[stat:~70%](of websites use PHP in some way, so when a serious vulnerability affects PHP itself, the potential impact can be pretty significant.)

To understand PHP2Shell, we only need three ideas: **HTTP requests**, **memory**, and **pointers**.

## 📨 1. HTTP requests

Whenever you log in, search for a product, or add something to your basket, your browser sends an HTTP request to the server to tell it what you want to do. If the website uses PHP, the PHP runtime helps process it.

[widget:request-flow]

## 🧠 2. Memory

A computer needs memory to work with that data. Think of memory as a **workspace**: when a program needs somewhere to store information temporarily, it allocates a section of memory, and once it's finished, it releases it so it can be reused.

## 👉 3. Pointers

A pointer is a variable that refers to a **location in memory**, like an address telling the program where to find a particular piece of data.

Normally everything works as expected: PHP **allocates** memory, **uses** it, and **releases** it. But what happens when something goes wrong with that process? That's where PHP2Shell comes in.

---

## 🐛 Bug #1: the half-filled form

The first problem happens when PHP **runs out of memory while it's setting up a request**. It can't finish, so some of its internal data structures are left only partly initialised.

Think of it like starting to fill in a form but running out of time halfway through:

[widget:half-filled-form]

If another part of the program later assumes the form is complete, it interprets the unfinished information incorrectly, and things start behaving in unexpected ways.

## 👻 Bug #2: use-after-free

Remember pointers? Imagine PHP has finished with a piece of memory and released it, but another part of the program **still holds a reference to that old location**. That memory may already be reused for something else. Step through it:

[widget:use-after-free]

[reveal:So are the two bugs the same thing?](Not quite! Bug #1 is about **incomplete initialisation** after a memory allocation fails. Bug #2 is about **using memory after it's been released**. Different causes, but both leave PHP handling its internal data in an unsafe way.)

---

## 🎯 Where the attacker comes in

An attacker may send **specially crafted HTTP requests** designed to trigger these bugs. If the right conditions are met, here's how it can unfold:

[widget:attack-chain]

**Remote code execution** sounds complicated, but the idea is simple: the attacker gets a remote computer (here, the web server) to run code *they* chose. What happens next depends on the permissions the PHP process has and what other protections are in place.

Imagine visiting what looks like a completely legitimate online shop. You choose your products, go to checkout and enter your card details, but the site has been compromised and the checkout page is fake 🛒💳

[callout:warning](That's just one *possible* result. **The vulnerability itself isn't a fake checkout page**, and it doesn't automatically give attackers every piece of information on the server.)

## 🔑 So why "no password needed"?

[flip:Hackers found a way to skip the login page](They never use the login page at all. They exploit the bug by sending requests straight to a vulnerable server, so the normal password check simply never comes into it.)

When people say hackers can get in without a password, they're describing the **result**, not the **mechanism**.

## 🛡️ Is every PHP website vulnerable?

No! Whether a website is affected depends on:
- the **PHP version** it's running
- whether the **fixes have been applied**
- how the **server is configured**

[callout:tip](This is why security warnings matter: administrators need to find affected systems, **apply the updates**, and check for signs they've already been compromised.)

---

## ✨ To sum up

What sounds like a simple headline, *"hackers can access websites without passwords"*, is actually a technical story about memory allocation, incomplete initialisation, use-after-free behaviour and potentially remote code execution, happening deep inside a language that a huge part of the web relies on.

So next time you come across a cybersecurity headline, ask one more question: **okay, but what actually went wrong?** 💭

title: Real-time Data Sensor Calibration | University of Nottingham - School of Computer Science
excerpt: A second-year Software Engineering group project carried out throughout the full academic year 25/26, supervised by Lucas Fonseca.
content:
[stats:At a glance](6|teammates ;; 8 months|of development ;; 13–16 ms|end-to-end latency (target: under 50 ms) ;; 60 Hz|live graph updates)

[callout:key](**TL;DR**: we built a real-time system that reads muscle signals (EMG), cleans and calibrates them for each person, and streams them live to a React dashboard. At demo day, people played a dino game and controlled a robot arm using only their muscles 🦾)

## Project Overview 📝

As part of the software engineering group project module at the University of Nottingham that ran across the full academic year, my team of 6 applied to three different projects, went through interviews, and ended up being the top applicant team for this project amongst several competing teams.

Real-Time Sensor Calibration (RTSC) was honestly one of the best projects we could have worked on. It brought together both software and hardware in a way that made the project feel truly real and meaningful. What started as an academic project slowly turned into something bigger — a system with real potential to continue being used and developed in future robotics research.

Below, you’ll find a more detailed overview of the project, my involvement throughout the year, and my reflections at the end of this journey :)

---

## EMG Background & Problem ‼️

EMG sensors detect the electrical activity produced by muscles during contraction. However, the raw signal produced is very noisy and differs from one person to another due to factors such as electrode placement, surrounding electrical interference, and natural differences in muscle activity, which makes it inconsistent to use directly.

Try it yourself 👇 hold the button (or drag the slider) to "flex", then switch between the raw, filtered and calibrated signal:

[widget:emg-playground]

---

## Hardware Components 💻

The project was originally intended to use research-grade Delsys EMG sensors for real-time robotic interaction and control. However, because access to the laboratory and equipment was limited throughout development, a large part of the project ended up being developed using the MyoWare 2.0 EMG muscle sensor instead.

The main hardware used throughout the project included:

- MyoWare 2.0 EMG Muscle Sensor connected with an ESP32 module to allow continuous EMG acquisition through a Bluetooth connection. Due to its accessibility and portability, this setup became the primary hardware used throughout most of the software development and testing process.
![small|right|soft](/blog-media/1778794768669-real-time-data-sensor-calibration-university-of-nottingham-school-of-computer-science-inline-0-1778827609289-tsj4f6.jpg)

![small|left|soft](/blog-media/1778794768669-real-time-data-sensor-calibration-university-of-nottingham-school-of-computer-science-inline-1-1778827610474-addm00.jpg)
- Delsys EMG Sensors, which were intended for the research-focused side of the project and integration with the Kinova Gen3 robotic arm for real-time muscle-based robotic control.
![small|left|soft](/blog-media/1778794768669-real-time-data-sensor-calibration-university-of-nottingham-school-of-computer-science-inline-2-1778827611782-5iga12.jpg)

![small|right|soft](/blog-media/1778794768669-real-time-data-sensor-calibration-university-of-nottingham-school-of-computer-science-inline-3-1778827612907-nsqgmo.jpg)
Both sensor systems were used for calibration workflows, live signal processing, JSON profile generation, and frontend interaction within the software.

---

## System Architecture 🏛️

The RTSC system architecture is built around real-time acquisition, processing, calibration, and visualisation of EMG sensor data. Live muscle signals are collected from the EMG sensor or replayed from recorded CSV samples, then processed through filtering and smoothing stages before being stored in a real-time buffer.

The backend manages sensor communication, calibration workflows, data processing, and reusable calibration profiles, while WebSocket streaming enables low-latency real-time communication with the frontend dashboard. The frontend provides live visualisation through interactive graphs, contraction feedback bars, calibration controls, and system monitoring tools, allowing users to interact with their muscle activity in real time.

[widget:rtsc-pipeline]

And here's the full architecture diagram:
![full|center|soft](/blog-media/1778794768669-real-time-data-sensor-calibration-university-of-nottingham-school-of-computer-science-inline-4-1778827614340-ktvtag.jpg)
---

## Calibration & Signal Processing Pipeline 📈📉
![full|center|soft](/blog-media/1778794768669-real-time-data-sensor-calibration-university-of-nottingham-school-of-computer-science-inline-5-1778827615674-5kg4qw.jpg)
---

## Frontend & User Interaction 👥

The frontend was developed using React and TypeScript with a strong focus on interactivity and user experience. A major part of the project was being able to calibrate and visualise live EMG signals in real time, which made the live graph one of the main elements and core focuses of the whole system. To keep the dashboard clean while still giving easy access to controls and features, different settings and tools were organised through the navigation bar located on the top left of the interface.

The calibration workflow was designed to feel guided and simple to follow, with audio SFX and live visual feedback helping users interact with the system more naturally during the calibration stages. For the final demo day, a small emulator-style game was also integrated into the software so people could interact with the system in a more engaging and fun way using their own muscle activity.

At the bottom of the dashboard, live system information and diagnostics were continuously displayed, including connection states, stream rate, backend rate, latency measurements, Band WebSocket status, and backend status. This helped monitor the overall performance and stability of the system in real time during both development and demonstrations.

---

## Technical Challenges 🚨

Real-time systems are unforgiving: every small change affects everything else. These were our biggest challenges (tap to open each group):

[stat:13–16 ms](end-to-end latency in the final system, comfortably below the **50 ms** project requirement ⚡)

[reveal:📶 Signal quality (3)](Noisy and inconsistent EMG signals caused by electrode placement, muscle differences, movement, and surrounding electrical interference. ;; Designing a reliable calibration workflow that could adapt to different users while keeping the system stable and responsive. ;; Creating hysteresis activation bands to reduce rapid fluctuations and false triggering during live interaction.)

[reveal:⚡ Real-time performance (4)](Balancing signal responsiveness and stability so the system reacted quickly without producing unstable or flickering outputs. ;; Maintaining low-latency real-time streaming and visualisation, with end-to-end latency typically remaining between 13 ms and 16 ms, comfortably below the 50 ms project requirement. ;; Handling continuous live updates at 60 Hz without causing frontend lag or unstable graph rendering. ;; Preventing unnecessary frontend rerenders and performance drops during continuous real-time graph updates.)

[reveal:🧱 Architecture (2)](Managing real-time synchronisation between live sensor acquisition, backend processing, WebSocket communication, and frontend rendering. ;; Designing a modular architecture where live sensors, replay systems, calibration workflows, backend processing, and frontend interaction could operate independently without affecting the stability of the rest of the system.)

[reveal:🔌 Hardware (2)](Bluetooth connectivity instability and sensor disconnections during long continuous streaming sessions. ;; Building a system flexible enough to support both lightweight consumer EMG hardware and research-grade sensor setups.)

---

## My Role Within the Project 👩‍💻

I was elected to be the team administrator, which gave me the responsibility of organising meetings, taking attendance, handling submissions and deadlines, and maintaining communication between the supervisor and the team. I also set up collaboration platforms such as Discord to improve communication and coordination throughout development.

Alongside that, I initially started working on the frontend and built the first simple prototype of the interface before it later evolved into the final real-time dashboard and visualisation system. I also contributed to parts of the backend, including the file manager system.

During the second semester, I took the MyoWare sensor home with me over the holidays to properly begin testing whether what we had built so far was fully functional in real conditions outside the laboratory environment. A large part of my contribution later focused on frontend interaction, calibration behaviour, latency monitoring, and improving the overall live user experience of the system.
![medium|center|soft](/blog-media/1778794768669-real-time-data-sensor-calibration-university-of-nottingham-school-of-computer-science-inline-6-1778827617004-5nv9xw.jpg)
Some of the main issues and improvements I worked on:

Tap each card to flip it from the issue 🐛 to the fix ✅

[fix:Bluetooth streaming stability issues where the connection consistently dropped after around 30 seconds of continuous streaming](Resolved by throttling excessive BLE notification flooding on the ESP32 side, improving desktop client stability while maintaining real-time streaming performance.)
[fix:The live graph and FlexBar occasionally displayed high or maximum activation immediately after connection, even while the user was relaxed](Refined the calibration baseline, activation range, and threshold behaviour to produce more stable live readings and interaction behaviour.)
[fix:Misleading latency measurements](Split displayed latency into backend latency and real stream latency instead of relying only on backend ping values.)
[fix:FlexBar behaving like a raw signal bar](Refactored the FlexBar to act as a calibrated activation display using the user’s saved MVC and relax calibration values instead of raw EMG values.)
[fix:Calibration workflow complexity](Removed the medium calibration stage since the MyoWare sensor struggled to consistently distinguish between medium and maximum contractions, making the workflow more reliable and user-friendly.)
[fix:Missing relax baseline data affecting calibration accuracy](Fixed calibration handling so relax baseline values were correctly included within saved calibration results.)
[fix:Hysteresis band calculation instability](Refined hysteresis band generation to use contraction stage averages and activation ranges instead of unstable max-only calculations.)
[fix:Calibration values occasionally being shared across users](Corrected user-specific calibration loading and storage behaviour to isolate profiles properly.)
[fix:Latency and stale sensor updates affecting live visualisation](Reduced unnecessary rebroadcasting of stale sensor samples to improve graph responsiveness and streaming stability.)
[fix:Graph display and live signal behaviour becoming unstable during streaming](Improved live graph rendering, scaling behaviour, and frontend interaction to maintain smoother real-time visualisation.)

## After 8 Months of RTSC 💗

As much as this project was time-consuming, all the development, knowledge, and personal growth I gained throughout it feels priceless 🤍 It taught me how even the smallest changes in a real-time system can affect the entire logic and behaviour of the software.

The project also taught me the responsibility of always staying on top of things to make sure we delivered work on time while maintaining a high standard throughout development 🔥 Working on a system that combined hardware, backend processing, frontend interaction, and real-time streaming made me grow technically far more than I expected at the beginning of the year.

I also discovered something important about myself during this project: I genuinely like my work to feel unique. Whenever I felt something was missing, I could not leave it unfinished until I found a way to improve or refine it. As normal as I once thought my creative side was, the feedback and comments I received from my teammates throughout the project made me realise that I do have my own unique way of presenting ideas, interactions, and user experiences 💞

Looking back now, RTSC became much more than just a university project. It was one of the first projects that truly made me feel what real software engineering, collaboration, debugging, creativity, and problem-solving look like in practice.

I would also like to thank our supervisor, Lucas Fonseca, who genuinely made this project experience even better. His support, feedback, and encouragement throughout the year helped the team constantly improve and push the project further.

## Demo Day & Showcase 👾🦾

As part of the module, we had to present our final software and aim to leave a strong impression on all visitors, including academics, sponsors, supervisors, and students.

Our final demonstration almost felt like two different projects combined into one system due to the different hardware setups and interactions we showcased:

- The MyoWare setup was connected to an integrated emulator where muscle contractions controlled a classic dinosaur-style game. Reaching a specific activation threshold triggered a keyboard spacebar press, while relaxing below another threshold released the input, allowing users to control the game entirely through muscle activity.
[video:short](https://youtube.com/shorts/skcaQnN4n3Y?si=Gx3DH650KSqPxBLz)
- The Delsys setup was demonstrated alongside the Kinova Gen3 robotic arm. Different contraction bands controlled the robot gripper in real time: relaxing opened the gripper, medium contraction held the object, and maximum contraction closed the gripper. This allowed the robot to pick up a cap, move it across an obstacle , and place it into another location through EMG-controlled interaction.
[video:short](https://youtube.com/shorts/6Us6lDBx-PE?si=tFpgoKCflhTfkr74)
One of the most rewarding parts of the showcase was seeing people interact with the system in real time and realise that the project combined live signal processing, calibration, robotics, frontend interaction, and hardware control into one fully working system!

title: AI Is Starting to Move Into the Physical World
excerpt: Recent robotics news shows AI moving beyond screens and into machines that can learn, move, and act in real spaces.
content:
## Why this caught my attention
A lot of AI news still focuses on chatbots, image generators, and software agents. But one of the most interesting shifts happening right now is that AI is starting to move into the physical world.

---

## From language to action
Recent robotics news makes that clear. Meta has acquired a humanoid robotics startup to strengthen its work on AI for robots, while Boston Dynamics is working with Google DeepMind on the next generation of Atlas. The interesting part is not only the hardware. It is the idea that robots may need foundation models of their own: systems trained to understand movement, objects, space, and physical interaction.

> Intelligence becomes more than prediction. It becomes action.

That changes how I think about AI. A chatbot can be wrong and correct itself in text, but a robot acting in the real world has to deal with gravity, friction, timing, safety, and uncertainty. Intelligence becomes more than prediction. It becomes action.

## Why robotics feels exciting
This is why robotics feels like one of the most exciting areas of AI. It combines perception, language, control, planning, and real-world feedback. It also shows how difficult "general intelligence" really is. Understanding a sentence is one challenge. Understanding how to pick up a fragile object, navigate a room, or work safely near people is another.

For me, this is the kind of AI progress worth watching: not just models that can answer questions, but systems that can eventually help in homes, hospitals, factories, and everyday environments.
